Rentrée tendue à McGill: Tense Start to the School Year at McGill
Pour les étudiants qui fréquentent l’Uni: For students at McGill University, this year's back-to-school season feels a little different.
Katz, de son surnom, participe à un rass: Katz, as she is nicknamed, takes part in a rally in front of the university's administration building. Photo: Melissa Haouari
Pour beaucoup des gens qui m’entourent (: For many of the people around me (and for me too), September means back to school. And for many in my circle, that means back to university. I immediately thought of McGill students, who went through a lot last year. Today, you might think the page has been turned and a new chapter is beginning for the institution, but the demons of the past still haunt McGill's grounds.
En me rendant sur les lieux à plusieurs: Having gone to campus several times during the first days of classes, I saw that a lot of frustration is still present among students. In the bathrooms, you could see partially torn-off pro-Palestinian stickers, phrases written in marker calling for a ceasefire and insulting remarks about Hamas. Pro-Palestinian and pro-Israeli messages have also been spray-painted on street signs.
Bref, il est clair qu’une tension existe: In short, it is clear that tension exists among students and that, despite the messages of hope and the calls for calm issued by the administration on the university's website, we are far from having opened any kind of dialogue or found common ground for the entire community.
Le plus difficile, dans la préparation d: The hardest part of preparing this story was finding Palestinian voices. Unfortunately, I could not find a single one who agreed to be interviewed. I was still able to speak with people who advocate for Palestinian rights, and I tried to understand how they view their return to McGill in such a tense climate. Many did not want to talk, others spoke in half-sentences, giving only a few specifics. Some were extremely careful during their interviews, meaning they thought three times before answering. It is obvious that speech was not free.
Pour cette rentrée 2024, beaucoup de squ: So for this 2024 back-to-school season, a lot of skeletons still seem to be hidden in the closets. What will the fall semester look like, nearly a year after the Hamas attack and the slaughter of Gazans by the Israeli army? How do the affected students feel? That is what I wanted to find out by going to campus.
La Converse vous amène donc sur le campu: La Converse takes you to the downtown campus, where students share their apprehensions about this new school year.
Bonne lecture et à bientôt !: Happy reading, and see you soon!
Le mois de septembre, qui marque le reto: For many people, September, the month that marks the return to school, means binders, pencils and books. For students at McGill University, this year's return is a little different. Over the past few months, the institution has been at the centre of several mobilizations and controversies. A pro-Palestinian encampment set up on university grounds, a hunger strike, numerous student demonstrations, injunction requests from the university… Today, when you walk through the Roddick Gates, the tension is palpable.
Impossible de ne pas remarquer les agent: It is impossible not to notice the security guards all over the grounds. The grass is green and fresh, and several trees stand on the muddy ground where, a few weeks ago, dozens of tents were set up.
Aujourd’hui, malgré la multiplication de: Today, despite the growing number of student demonstrations, the administration is struggling to be accountable.
De nombreux membres de la communauté jui: Many members of the Jewish community go to Café Plezl, located in the Maison Chabad McGill building, the campus synagogue. Photo: Melissa Haouari
À quelques pas du campus principal, bien: A few steps from the main campus, tucked away between the trees and the facades of the large buildings on Peel Street, is Café Plezl. What makes it unique is that it serves only kosher food.
Lorsqu’on y entre, on remarque tout de s: When you walk in, you immediately notice the large menu featuring a variety of Mediterranean cuisines and the few books written in Hebrew on the shelves along the walls. Sunlight pours in and brightens the room despite its basement location.
Nous sommes le mercredi 28 août, et c’es: It is Wednesday, August 28, the official first day of school for the McGill student community. The café is full, and we meet David*, who is starting his second year in economics.
Kippa sur la tête et étoile de David aut: With a kippah on his head and a Star of David around his neck, he proudly displays his Jewish identity. “I'm proud of who I am and I'm not afraid to show it,” he says as he sits down at one of the many tables. Yet for the past few months, he has no longer felt as comfortable as before.
« Je ne suis pas dupe. Je reçois beaucou: “I'm not naive. I get a lot of looks, I know that sometimes some people aren't comfortable with my presence,” he confides. Emotional, he tells us he is dreading going back to class. “It's a hard time for everyone. And I feel like the university should do more to protect the students who live at the centre of the tensions,” he says.
Ce qui déçoit l’étudiant, c’est que son: What disappoints the student is that his school is trying to compromise with people who, in his view, should not be consulted. “McGill shouldn't even try to negotiate with those who put up the encampment. Why is the university trying to compromise?” This is an allusion to the various attempts at talks between the administration and the organizers of the pro-Palestinian encampment set up on the institution's grounds for several months.
Selon lui, ce campement, où ont résonné: In his view, that encampment, where Palestinian liberation chants rang out, was a threat to his Jewish identity. “I have a huge amount of family in Israel. I just got back from there, actually. I talked to survivors of the October 7 attack, and when I see people from my school hanging a puppet in the likeness of the Jewish head of state in a striped uniform, I feel targeted.” He is referring to the discovery of <l1>a puppet with a photo of Benjamin Netanyahu's face stuck on it, hanged</l1> in front of the university's entrance. It was dressed in a black-and-white striped uniform, reminiscent of those worn by concentration camp prisoners.
David appréhende l’année scolaire qui ne: David is apprehensive about the school year that is just beginning, especially October 7. “I feel like it's going to be exhausting. I'm not really afraid of pro-Palestinian activists, but it's tiring to go to campus every day and see antisemitic phrases written on every wall.” This is a reference, in particular, to the slogan “From the river to the sea, Palestine will be free,” which he considers antisemitic, “because it doesn't recognize Israel's place in the Near East.”
Par-dessus tout, David espère que la ren: Above all, David hopes the school year will not start with violence. “I just want to go to class, be a normal student and not be afraid of getting dirty looks because of my kippah,” he concludes with a tired sigh.
Si certains jugent que le slogan « Du fl: While some believe the slogan “From the river to the sea” evokes the outright erasure of Israel, defenders of the Palestinian cause reject that interpretation and explain that <l1>the chant refers to a call for the liberation of occupied Palestine</l1> and to Palestinians' right to justice and equality.
Pourtant, pour des groupes de défense de: Yet for Jewish rights advocacy groups such as B'nai Brith or the Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs, the slogan is an “antisemitic call that advocates the ethnic cleansing of the Jewish people.” For other organizations, such as Independent Jewish Voices, “these words encompass the many spaces in which Israel exercises control over Palestinians.” The chant represents a call to respect the freedom and human rights of Palestinians across their entire territory.
Pour en savoir davantage sur l’emploi de: To learn more about the use of this slogan, information is available on the website of <l1>Independent Jewish Voices</l1> and that of the <l2>Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs</l2>.
Sur le campus montréalais, on croise de: On the Montréal campus, you come across many students getting ready for their first classes. It is the start of a new adventure, or a return to the fold, which is the case for Kalinga, who is starting her fourth year at university.
Pour l’étudiante en kinésiologie, cette: For the kinesiology student, this return to school is, on the face of it, normal. But even though she expects the academic routine to prevail, she fears that the tension on campus will keep her from getting through her year.
Kalinga a suivi attentivement les événem: Kalinga followed last year's events closely, even though she attended her classes remotely. “I wasn't always on campus, but I felt affected by what was happening. Every time my school was in the media, it was for the same reasons. Now that the encampment has been dismantled, I'm afraid some students will be even more frustrated than last year,” she explains.
« J’espère juste être en mesure de termi: “I just hope I'll be able to finish the year without any problems,” she says, referring to the numerous demonstrations she saw every week last year.
En effet, depuis la fin du mois d’août,: Indeed, since the end of August, students have been mobilizing and already organizing rallies for their respective causes. That is the case for Katz*, who is taking part in one of the rallies held two days later.
Sur le campus de l’Université McGill, un: On the McGill University campus, a security perimeter has been set up where the pro-Palestinian encampment stood a few weeks ago. Photo: Melissa Haouari
Le 30 août donc, vers l’heure du dîner,: So on August 30, around lunchtime, the first walk out** of the school year gets under way. About a hundred students gather in front of the James Administration Building, which houses the institution's senior management and secretariat.
Katz est une des étudiantes juives qui é: Katz is one of the Jewish students at McGill. She insists that the goal of this demonstration is not to point the finger at the Jewish community, of which she is a part.
Membre du chapitre mcgillois de Voix jui: A member of the McGill chapter of Independent Jewish Voices, the young woman believes it is imperative that the administration take activists' demands seriously. “Several organizations are coming together on the same point: boycotting and divesting the university's millions of dollars from companies that are involved, directly or indirectly, in the massacre being carried out in Gaza,” she says through the red keffiyeh covering her face. She is firm: “The administration must hear us. It won't be able to keep ignoring us for long.”
« Les étudiants qui ne se sentent pas à: “Students who don't feel comfortable with our actions don't have to listen to us, but they must obey the law,” she continues. “We want to study at a school where transparency, communication and accountability are at the heart of our relationships, both with the administration and with other students,” she adds.
L’étudiante ne comprend toujours pas pou: The student still does not understand why, despite every attempt at discussion, the administration has not responded to the demands of Solidarity for Palestinian Human Rights and Independent Jewish Voices, who have been “stubbornly talking to a wall for months,” she says.
Si Katz, comme nombre d’étudiants, se se: While Katz, like many students, feels frustrated, others are anxious. As the second week of classes begins at McGill, it is hard to find members of the Palestinian community willing to talk about their concerns.
Les étudiants rencontrés qui militent po: The students we met who are active in the Palestinian cause say they are afraid. Faces tense up as soon as we suggest an interview. Clearly, many are reluctant to talk to the media.
D’où vient cette méfiance ? « Elle ne so: Where does this mistrust come from? “It doesn't come out of nowhere,” says Salma*, a student we met on campus. She limits what she shares about herself, “for safety reasons,” she tells us right away.
« Aujourd’hui plus que jamais, les étudi: “Today more than ever, students don't trust anyone, especially journalists or people who represent a political or academic institution,” Salma continues.
La crainte de sanctions de la part de l’: Fear of sanctions from the institution plays a part: “Nobody knows what could happen to them if they show up somewhere or speak publicly.”
That fear doesn't come out of nowhere. Last June, the administration sent the entire student community a <l1>statement</l1> in which it declared that “those [who took part in the encampment] will face the full range of sanctions prescribed by the school's policy.” That decision followed the rejection of a mediation offer the university had made earlier.
Dans ce communiqué, l’institution exprim: In the same statement, the institution also expressed its “intention to explore the legal measures available to [it] to recover the costs associated with the damage [it] sustained.”
« On ne sait pas si la direction va sanc: “We don't know if the administration will sanction people who speak out. People are afraid because they don't want to see their academic path go up in smoke because of a statement they might make to the media or to police, for example,” Salma explains. “All of that is pressure, and it wears us out.”
D’autre part, la présence d’agents de sé: On top of that, the presence of security guards on campus gives the impression of being “constantly under surveillance,” she continues.
Elle est consciente que, depuis qu’elle: She is aware that, since she started wearing a keffiyeh, people at school look at her. But now, she says she feels watched. “As if they were analyzing my every move,” she says. She even realized one day that someone was filming her. “When I set foot on campus, sometimes I get followed and filmed by other people.”
Pourtant, Salma est loin d’être la seule: Yet Salma is far from the only one wearing a keffiyeh. Near the Palestinian flag flying at the campus entrance, a few students proudly wear theirs, and some use them to cover their faces. Here too, very few want to talk. “I don't want to say too much, but I can tell you I'm very frustrated,” says Nesrine*.
L’étudiante entame sa dernière année d’u: The student is starting her final year of university. Despite the little she agrees to share about herself, we learn that she is of Lebanese origin and that she is actively involved in the fight for Palestinian rights.
« Plus le temps passe, plus je suis tann: “The more time goes by, the more fed up I get,” she tells us. “McGill doesn't listen to its students. How long are we going to have to keep chanting that we disagree with the administration?” she asks, out of breath.
Alors que nous nous promenons à ses côté: As we walk beside her along the campus's central path, she opens up a little more. She is active in the pro-Palestinian movement, which has been growing in the city since last October. She believes it is necessary to “educate the next generations of students so that future administrations don't do the same thing again.”
D’un ton plus que ferme, la jeune Montré: In a more than firm tone, the young Montrealer states the following: “Let's be clear: we can't stay silent. We can't take part in what our school is doing. We can't do nothing when we see that our money is being used to fund a war machine like Israel,” she says, alluding to the tuition fees paid by students.
Nesrine est persuadée que, si l’universi: Nesrine is convinced that if the university does not respond to the protesters' demands, the tension will only rise. She is not alone in thinking so. Even several days after the August 30 walk out, students are still showing up in front of the university's administration building to chant pro-Palestinian slogans in front of security guards.
Des étudiants se regroupent devant le pa: Students gather in front of the James Building to make themselves heard by the administration, in the presence of security guards posted at the entrance. Photo: Melissa Haouari
Montrée du doigt par plusieurs étudiants: Pointed at by several students, the university's administration refuses to comment at all on the tension that persists on campus. The administration, which did not want to answer our questions, referred us to the press releases it had published a few days earlier.
Le recteur de l’établissement, Deep Sain: In them, the university's principal, Deep Saini, highlights the “enthusiastic and lively” nature of the start of the school year. He makes little mention of the tensions that remain on site and instead describes a return to school taking place against a backdrop of “various difficulties in Quebec, in Canada and elsewhere in the world, which have a direct impact on the university and members of its community.”
En juillet dernier, le recteur demandait: Last July, the principal asked the student body to engage in peaceful dialogue. He described the university as a “laboratory of ideas” where “teaching, learning and research activities (...) must take place in a climate conducive to frank discussions, conducted openly and respectfully, even on the most difficult subjects.”
Reste à voir comment l’université compte: It remains to be seen how the university intends to go about ensuring a climate conducive to frank discussions.
*Le prénom a été modifié afin de préserv: *The first name has been changed to protect the anonymity of the students whose accounts we gathered.
**Un <em>walk out</em> étudiant se produ: **A student walk out happens when students leave their classes at the same time to show their discontent over a particular cause.
